title: Northern Wei
capsule: Northern Wei was a Tuoba Xianbei dynasty that ruled northern China from 386 to 534 AD, the most durable and powerful of the Sixteen Kingdoms era successors that fragmented after the Western Jin collapse. Emperor Taiwu (r. 423–452) unified the north by 439, defeating the Northern Liang and ending the era of competing northern states; Emperor Xiaowen (r. 471–499) carried out a celebrated Sinicisation programme, relocating the capital from Datong to Luoyang in 494, mandating Chinese dress and language at court, and encouraging intermarriage with Chinese aristocratic families. Northern Wei was a major conduit for Buddhism in China, sponsoring the Yungang and Longmen cave sculpture complexes. A military revolt of frontier garrison troops (the Six Garrisons Rebellion, 524–530) fractured the state; by 534 it had split into the Eastern Wei and Western Wei under rival generals.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Northern Wei's territory in northern China is well attested by the dynasty's own administrative geography (the zhou-commandery system) and court annals compiled in the Weishu; the steppe frontiers to the north against the Rouran Khaganate were militarized zones rather than fixed lines.
